processing: Fresh leaf from wild Hainan large-leaf plants is made as a green tea: fixed by heat, rolled and dried. Black tea is also made in the same district, but that is a different product.
harvest_season: No specific picking calendar is recorded for Shuiman. The Hainan large-leaf plant buds from early February, far earlier than mainland gardens.
appearance_dry: Little is recorded; typical of large-leaf green tea, expect fairly bold, dark green twisted leaf.
appearance_liquor: Typical of green tea, a clear yellow-green, likely a little deeper than small-leaf greens.
appearance_wet: Typical of large-leaf green tea: broad, thick, olive-green leaves.
taste_profile: Known for a strong sweet return and for holding up over many steeps. Expect more body and grip than a delicate small-leaf green, as is usual with large-leaf plants.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for large-leaf green tea. Cooler water and short steeps keep the bitterness down; it is known for lasting through several infusions.

vintage_note: As with other Chinese greens, it is sold and best drunk as the current year's harvest; no vintage system is documented. Hainan's early picking means new tea arrives ahead of the mainland, so check the picking date. Local black tea from Wuzhishan is sold separately under its own name.
description:
Shuiman Cha is a green tea named after Shuiman township in Wuzhishan, in the mountains of central Hainan. What makes it unusual is the raw material: wild plants of the Hainan large-leaf type, a tree-form tea in a tropical rainforest setting, and not the small-leaf bushes behind most Chinese greens.

The making is ordinary green tea work: fix, roll, dry. The difference comes from the leaf. Large leaves carry more body and bitterness than small-leaf ones, so this will not taste like a Long Jing.

It is praised for a strong sweet return and for how many steeps it takes. Little else is recorded in detail about the cup. Go easy on water temperature and steep time at first, then lengthen as it fades.

When buying, make sure you know which tea you are getting. Wuzhishan today is better known for black tea, and most current writing about the district is about that. Ask for the green and for its picking date, and treat the word wild with some care, since it is an easy claim to make and hard to check.
history:
The name goes back further than the current industry. A Ming gazetteer of Hainan, the Qiongtai Zhi, is reported to name the tea of Shuiman at Wuzhishan as the island's best known, from trees so thick they took an embrace to circle; retellings differ on the edition and the detail. A Qing county gazetteer of Ding'an is reported to rank it first among the Li mountain teas, and it is said to have served as tribute in that period.

Modern production came later. State tea farming arrived in Wuzhishan around the late 1950s and focused heavily on black tea, and the green tea has since gained a place among Hainan's named teas.
